headline: Finding meaningful controls inside a GAN
intro: Moving a GAN’s latent code can change a face dramatically. I studied whether discovered directions change one interpretable attribute consistently across generated images.
context: University of Michigan · Machine-learning course research · Jan–Sept 2021
role: Human-evaluation design and execution, annotator recruitment, results analysis, shared algorithm implementation, and report coauthorship.

hero.alt: Three generated StyleGAN2 faces show the same latent identity with a closed, partly open, and widely open mouth.
hero.caption: A real editing sweep from Figure 1: the middle image is the original latent code; the sides move in opposite directions.
hero.credit: Chen, Qin, Bi, Chen and Zhao · 2021 course report

question.title: Does a direction mean the same thing across images?
question.text: A striking edit is only a starting point. I designed the human evaluation to examine whether each direction produced an interpretable, consistent change, then analyzed the comparison.

steps.title: Discover
steps.text: Co-implemented FastICA factorization of pretrained generator weights, building on SeFa to discover directions without training another neural network.

steps.title: Inspect
steps.text: Generated editing sweeps and compared similar attributes in StyleGAN2 trained on FFHQ. Looked for changes that preserve unrelated characteristics.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.text: Recruited eight annotators, designed and ran the mean-opinion-score study, and analyzed the selected directions. The team also examined semantic correlations with CLIP.

gallery.alt: Side-by-side ICA-SeFa and SeFa examples compare hair-color and glasses editing directions across five generated faces per strip.
gallery.caption: Selected hair-color and glasses examples from Figure 4. Each strip follows one direction; the center image is the shared starting point.

finding.title: Evaluation makes interpretability visible.
finding.text: Selected ICA-SeFa directions showed clearer attribute control in the qualitative comparisons and higher top-ranked human scores. Because the study rated a manually selected subset, these findings should not be read as an average over every discovered direction.

details: The public course experiment discovered 200 directions per method, selected 35 per method for human rating, and reported the ten highest-scoring directions. Mean opinion scores represent human judgments, not classification accuracy.
CLIP analysis provided a complementary view of how directions correlated with named attributes. It was team research implemented by Dongyang Zhao.
credits: Houming Chen proposed the idea, developed the theory and algorithm, and led implementation. Le Qin owned the human-evaluation work and contributed to implementation. Yutong Bi and Jiaxi Chen contributed literature review and theory development.
Visuals come from the linked 2021 course report. The full course presentation remains available in the project resources.
